title: Sauerkraut
subtitle: Fermented white cabbage, sharp, funky, and made with only salt
excerpt: Sauerkraut is white cabbage fermented with just salt. The cabbage produces its own brine and ferments over 1 to 4 weeks at room temperature. No vinegar, no cooking, no special equipment needed.
sourceNotes: Central European fermentation tradition, widely made across Germany, Poland, and the Alsace region. Two-percent salt by weight of cabbage is the standard fermentation ratio.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Ferment for 1–4 weeks at room temperature. Refrigerate to stop fermentation at desired sourness.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fermentation by naturally occurring lactobacillus bacteria on the vegetable surface. Salt inhibits harmful bacteria while these beneficial bacteria produce lactic acid, preserving the food and creating its sour flavour.

content.text: Sauerkraut is made with two ingredients: white cabbage and salt. The salt draws moisture from the cabbage and creates a brine that the naturally occurring bacteria on the cabbage surface use to
the whole jar. There is no vinegar, no cooking, and no special equipment,  just salt, time, and a weight to keep the cabbage submerged.
The standard ratio is 2% salt by weight of cabbage. Get that right and the rest is just waiting.

items.prepNote: non-iodised, 2% of cabbage weight. Iodised salt inhibits fermentation.

content.text: Weigh the shredded cabbage and weigh out exactly 2% of that weight in non-iodised salt. Toss together in a large bowl. Squeeze and massage the cabbage firmly with both hands for 5 to 10 minutes until it releases a significant amount of liquid and collapses in volume. The cabbage must produce enough brine to submerge itself,  if it does not, dissolve 1 tsp salt in 200 ml water and add just enough to cover.

Pack the cabbage and all its liquid firmly into a clean jar. Add the caraway seeds if using. Press down hard so the brine rises above the cabbage. The cabbage must stay below the brine surface throughout fermentation,  above the brine is where spoilage occurs. Use a reserved outer cabbage leaf folded to fit the jar as a weight, or a small clean plastic bag filled with brine to hold everything down. Cover the jar with a cloth secured with a rubber band to allow gases to escape.

Leave at room temperature (18 to 22 °C) for 1 to 4 weeks. Check daily for the first few days,  push the cabbage down if it rises above the brine, and taste from day 7. The sauerkraut will bubble (this is normal and good) and develop sourness gradually. At 1 week it is mild; at 4 weeks it is properly sour. Refrigerate when the sourness is to your taste,  refrigeration slows fermentation almost completely.

items.symptom: No liquid after 24 hours of salting
items.cause: Cabbage didn't release enough moisture, or too little salt.
items.fix: Dissolve 1 tsp non-iodised salt in 200 ml water and add just enough to cover the cabbage. Check the salt ratio, it must be 2% of the cabbage weight.

items.symptom: White scum or foam on the surface
items.cause: Normal byproduct of fermentation, kahm yeast.
items.fix: Skim it off and discard. It is not harmful but can add off-flavours if left in. Ensure the cabbage stays below the brine.

items.symptom: Pink or red discolouration with bad smell
items.fix: Discard and start again. Ensure everything is clean and the cabbage was fully submerged throughout.

items.cause: Temperature too cold (below 15 °C), or iodised salt used.
items.fix: Move to a warmer spot. Iodised salt kills the bacteria needed for fermentation, always use non-iodised.

content.text: Refrigerate once fermented to your taste. Keeps for 6 months in the fridge, submerged in its brine.
